e.t: This Hebrew word is the proper name “Ephraim.” It identifies Ephraim as a named person, people, or tribal designation rather than expressing a general quality or action. The name is used throughout the Hebrew Old Testament, from Genesis through Zechariah, with 180 occurrences in this corpus. Its uses connect with genealogy, territorial identity, and the history of Israel, so its precise reference depends on the surrounding passage. It is consistently rendered “Ephraim” in the available English renderings.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to a ceremonial headpiece, rendered “diadem” or “mitre.” It names an item associated with honor or official appearance, rather than an action or quality. The word occurs six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in Job, Isaiah, and Zechariah. Its use in Isaiah and Zechariah especially connects it with a person’s recognized status and presentation. The precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “dung,” the waste material produced by animals. It is a concrete noun describing something used or handled as an object rather than an action or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in one verse in Ezekiel. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning remains the physical substance itself.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to “wheels,” naming a physical object rather than an action or quality. It occurs twice in the Old Testament, in Exodus and Jeremiah, and functions as the object connected with other actions or statements. Its normal sense is therefore concrete and practical: a movable, rounded part used with something else. The exact force in each passage depends on the surrounding verse and its immediate context.

This Hebrew word refers to seeking or practicing divination—attempting to obtain hidden knowledge or guidance through supernatural means. It is rendered “divination” and “divine,” and its uses include people who practice such things as well as the act itself. In the Old Testament, it occurs 23 times, especially in passages warning against forbidden spiritual practices or describing those who rely on them. Its precise role depends on the sentence in which it appears.

This Hebrew word means “near,” describing someone or something that is close by or within nearby reach. It marks physical proximity rather than distance, and its exact sentence role depends on how it is used in context. The word occurs nine times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in Ezra and Daniel. Its repeated use in Daniel includes descriptions of people coming near or being present close to someone. This ordinary sense remains consistent across its recorded occurrences.

This Hebrew word means “height,” referring to how high something rises or stands. It functions as a concise term for vertical elevation, whether describing a structure or something that extends upward. The word occurs five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in Ezra and Daniel. Its repeated rendering as “height” supports this central sense without requiring a broader range of meanings. The surrounding verse determines what object or feature is being measured or described.

This word expresses a limited idea whose exact sense depends on its context. It appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Judges 5:30, so Scripture gives little repeated usage by which to clarify its ordinary range. The available material does not preserve an explicit gloss or translation rendering. Its precise meaning should therefore be drawn from the surrounding verse and passage rather than expanded beyond what that context establishes.

This Hebrew noun refers to “mufflers,” an item of clothing. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at Isaiah 3:19. Its precise role in that sentence depends on the surrounding context. As a noun, it identifies a tangible article rather than an action, quality, or abstract idea. The word therefore names something worn or used as part of dress, while the single occurrence does not provide enough context to explain its particular appearance or purpose there.

This word is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Raphu.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew corpus, it occurs once, in Numbers 13:9. Because no explicit definition is available, its ordinary meaning is best understood as the person’s name, not as a common noun. Its precise significance beyond that name cannot be established from the available lexical information.

e.t: The word means “rest.” It refers to a recognized period set apart for ceasing from ordinary work, especially in passages concerning Israel’s appointed days of rest. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 11 times, primarily in Exodus and Leviticus. Its use is connected with instructions about observing, honoring, and keeping this rest, showing that it describes more than general relaxation: it identifies a designated time when ordinary labor stops. “Bottom” refers to the lowest part or underside of something. In this Hebrew Old Testament word, that is the only supported meaning, and it occurs once, in Daniel 6:24. The word therefore identifies a physical lower part rather than expressing an action or quality. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense remains “bottom.”

This Hebrew word means “bowed.” It describes a lowered or bent position and functions as a verb, expressing the act of bending downward or being brought into such a position. It occurs four times in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, including descriptions connected with a person, the soul, or a dwelling place. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Hebrew word is an identifying term, but its precise English meaning cannot be established from the available information. It appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Numbers 26:31. No short definition, approved meaning term, or English rendering is available, so it would be unsafe to expand the word into a more specific translation or description. Its exact sense must therefore be determined from the verse and its surrounding context rather than from this word entry alone.

This Hebrew verb means “keep.” It describes holding something in careful attention, guarding it, or faithfully observing what is entrusted or commanded. The word is used 468 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its basic idea covers both protecting something and maintaining faithful obedience. Its uses include keeping God’s words, observing instructions, and guarding what has been placed under one’s care. The surrounding sentence determines which aspect is most prominent.

Shaalim is a Hebrew proper name used for a place or region. It is rendered “Shaalim” and appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Samuel 9:4. Because the available wording preserves the name rather than translating it as an ordinary descriptive term, its meaning is primarily geographic identification: it names Shaalim. The surrounding verse is needed to explain its specific role in that passage.

Sharai is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Sharai” in English. It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. This name occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at Ezra 10:40. Because no explicit definition or broader usage is recorded, its plain lexical role is simply as the name by which that individual is identified. The surrounding verse supplies the context for understanding the person mentioned there.

Saraph is a Hebrew name rendered “Saraph,” identifying a particular person rather than expressing a general quality or action. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 4:22. Since the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s exact role in that sentence cannot be expanded beyond its name function. Its consistent rendering as “Saraph” supports treating it as a proper name within this occurrence.

e.t: Tikvath is a Hebrew proper name identifying someone mentioned in 2 Chronicles 34:22. It is not presented here as a general word describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, both times in that same verse, and its normal function is to identify a person in the account. The precise role of the person named Tikvath depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here.

This Hebrew word means “wonder.” It describes a response of astonishment or amazement when someone encounters something unexpected, overwhelming, or difficult to understand. In its nine Old Testament occurrences, it can describe people reacting with amazement, and it can also function in descriptions of situations that provoke such a response. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word means “troubled.” It describes a person or people thrown into inner distress, alarm, or agitation, and it functions as an action word rather than simply naming a feeling. Its 39 Old Testament occurrences show this broad use: people can be troubled, and circumstances can produce that unsettled response. The word appears from Genesis through Zephaniah, including passages involving fear, pressure, haste, and being driven into distress. The surrounding verse determines the specific form that this troubling takes.

Betonim is a Hebrew proper name, referring to a named location rather than expressing an ordinary action, quality, or object. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Joshua 13:26, and is rendered as “Betonim.” Because no explicit definition or surrounding verse text is available here, the word is best understood simply as the location’s name. Its precise significance in Joshua depends on the geographic context of that passage.
